episodes.title: The company building underwater drones for $50,000

keyPoints.title: Seagrass restoration is a major early focus with broad ecological impact
keyPoints.detail: Seagrass restoration addresses critical habitat loss impacting fish stocks and carbon sequestration, with Ulysses automating seed collection and planting as an initial use case.

keyPoints.title: Surface vehicle Leviathan enables endurance and communications
keyPoints.detail: Leviathan, an autonomous surface ship with a 2,000 nautical mile range, carries, charges, and communicates with underwater drones via acoustic modems and Starlink, managing limited underwater bandwidth issues.

keyPoints.title: Modular underwater robots enable flexibility and rapid adaptation
keyPoints.detail: The Mako vehicle is constructed from Lego-like modules to add batteries, thrusters, sonar, or cameras as needed, allowing customization for diverse maritime tasks and faster iteration.

keyPoints.title: Manufacturing verticalization is critical for scaling from hundreds to millions
keyPoints.detail: Ulysses is transitioning from off-the-shelf parts to in-house production, planning one of the largest underwater drone factories to meet demand far exceeding current maritime component suppliers' capacities.

episodes.synthesis: Ulysses, co-founded by Will O'Brien, is innovating in the underdeveloped sector of underwater robotics by building affordable, modular underwater drone systems designed to scale to millions of units. The company started focusing on seagrass restoration, a critical but overlooked ecological task that impacts 20% of ocean carbon sequestration and fisheries, due to habitat loss and overfishing threatening fish stocks by the 2040s. They developed an autonomous surface vehicle, Leviathan, which deploys the underwater drone Mako to perform diverse tasks such as mapping, seed collection, and cleanup, leveraging a modular design allowing for tailored sensor and propulsion setups. Ulysses aims for dramatic cost reductions, selling base underwater vehicles at around $50,000, which is two orders of magnitude cheaper than traditional options like those costing $5 million, enabling new use cases in…
episodes.whatChanged: Ulysses is delivering modular, autonomous underwater drones at $50,000 each, 100x cheaper than existing military-grade options, and scaling manufacturing to supply a market transitioning from episodic to persistent ocean operations.
episodes.whyItMatters: This massive cost reduction and scalable architecture enables new commercial and defense applications previously cost-prohibitive, effectively opening the ocean economy akin to how reusable rockets opened space, offering significant growth and strategic opportunities for defense, offshore energy, and ocean…

episodes.title: Jensen Huang | Does AI Revenue Justify Capex, '27 AI Bottlenecks, Singularity, Open vs Closed & more

keyPoints.title: Safety vs Speed in AI Development: Airbags Analogy
keyPoints.detail: Huang uses the airbags analogy to emphasize that AI safety measures should protect without slowing down progress, highlighting the delicate balance of rapid innovation and responsible governance.

keyPoints.title: America’s Three-Legged Stool for AI Leadership
keyPoints.detail: He articulates a strategic framework for US AI competitiveness based on compute, data availability, and talent, which underpins national policy and corporate strategy in AI development.

keyPoints.title: 2027 AI Bottlenecks: Compute and Power Constraints
keyPoints.detail: Huang highlights that 2027 will face a bottleneck of 50 GW of chips and 35 GW of power for AI to scale, underscoring physical and supply-side limits that the industry must overcome to sustain growth.

keyPoints.title: SpaceX and Data Centers in Orbit Concept
keyPoints.detail: The episode explores the novel idea of leveraging SpaceX’s capabilities to place data centers in orbit, potentially overcoming terrestrial energy and thermal challenges for scaling AI infrastructure.

episodes.synthesis: Jensen Huang provides a comprehensive overview of where AI stands approaching 2027, emphasizing how AI revenue streams can justify the substantial capital expenditure needed for the next generation of AI infrastructure. He identifies power constraints and the compute build-out bottleneck as major challenges facing AI's advancement, with NVIDIA projecting a need for 50 GW of chips and 35 GW of power to meet demand. Huang connects these technical challenges to broader strategic considerations, including responsibly accelerating technology development, the singularity's proximity, and the balance between open and closed AI models, arguing that managing these aspects well is critical for America’s competitive edge in AI.

episodes.whyItMatters: This bottleneck sets a concrete technological and investment challenge that informs capital expenditure decisions by AI infrastructure providers like NVIDIA and influences national strategic frameworks for AI leadership.

episodes.whatChanged: Digital dating algorithms now play a critical role in matchmaking effectiveness by focusing intensely on profile quality and user engagement signals.

episodes.synthesis: Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev outlines a bold vision for embedding AI-driven trading agents directly into retail investors' portfolios, expecting these AI 'agents' to handle trading complexities beyond typical individual capacity and to become a growing share of trading activity within the Robinhood app. He stresses that simply having the same AI tools won't provide an edge; differentiation arises from the unique data users feed their agents, the additional tools they integrate, and multi-asset strategies they deploy. This sets a foundation for personalized AI trading rather than a one-size-fits-all model.
episodes.whatChanged: Robinhood plans to integrate AI trading agents that manage user trades in separate accounts with tailored strategies, aiming to become a dominant part of retail trading activity.
episodes.whyItMatters: This integration offers retail investors access to complex, AI-driven trading previously available only to professionals, potentially transforming retail investing by enabling personalized automated strategies and increasing market participation. keyPoints.detail: SpaceX's latest spectrum purchase highlights a clear strategy to expand beyond satellite internet into distributed cellular networks integrated with its Starlink constellation.

episodes.title: David Vélez - Building Nubank and the Future of Global Banking - [Invest Like the Best, EP.495]

keyPoints.title: Nubank serves 140 million customers in Latin America
keyPoints.detail: David Vélez shares that Nubank has grown to serve 140 million customers, highlighting its large scale and data base for AI-driven banking.

keyPoints.title: Banking is still in its Blockbuster era
keyPoints.detail: Vélez argues most banking still happens in branches of incumbent banks, showing the industry’s low digital penetration and opportunity for fintech disruption.

keyPoints.title: Nubank’s AI organizational overhaul
keyPoints.detail: After missing the early moment of AI technology adoption, Nubank rebuilt its organization around AI, massively improving efficiency relative to incumbents.

keyPoints.title: U.S. market seen as primed for disruption
keyPoints.detail: Vélez targets the U.S. market, dominated by big banks, to introduce Nubank’s AI-driven digital service model as a competitive alternative.

Nubank, serving 140 million customers in Latin America, rebuilt its entire organizational model around AI after initially missing the critical moment when artificial intelligence matured and began proving effective. This organizational pivot is central to Nubank's efficiency and competitive edge against traditional banks. Vélez believes AI is the transformative force that will render digital banks dramatically more efficient than legacy incumbents, reshaping global banking standards.

keyPoints.title: Meta's $100B AI Bet on Muse Wonder
keyPoints.detail: Zuckerberg describes the decision late last year to invest $100-200 billion in Muse Wonder despite uncertainty about its success, illustrating the high-stakes nature of Meta's AI investment.

keyPoints.title: Multimodal Agent Coaching MMA

keyPoints.title: Active Memory and Active Focus Innovations
keyPoints.detail: Alexandr Wang explains Muse Wonder's 'active memory' for persistent, long-term recall, and 'active focus' enabling handling complex, multi-step tasks, key improvements over prior models.

keyPoints.title: Alignment as Instruction and Discretion
keyPoints.detail: Meta's alignment philosophy focuses on aligning AI behavior to the individual user's intent and values with high discretion, rather than generic moral constraints, differentiating it from other AI labs.

episodes.synthesis: The central argument in this episode is that Meta's AI division, led by Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang, is making a bold bet with the development and scale-up of their Muse Wonder model and agent product, representing a major $100 billion+ investment. Unlike many industry peers focused narrowly on coding or text-based tasks, Meta is building a highly multimodal AI agent that not only uses text but image, video, and voice inputs and outputs to operate as a proactive agent across many domains, including personal coaching, shopping, and professional tasks. The process involves a tightly-knit, small team at Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) emphasizing talent density over headcount, producing frontier models alongside methodical research and large infrastructure investments like the gigawatt-scale Prometheus and Hyperion clusters. This is a high-risk, high-reward strategy: Meta bet…
episodes.whatChanged: Meta announced the Muse Wonder model, a significantly larger multimodal AI agent designed to serve as a personal and professional AI assistant with improved active memory, focus, and domain expertise, available both in the Muse app and via API.
episodes.whyItMatters: Muse Wonder’s innovations and Meta’s focused investment in a tight, talented team with massive compute infrastructure position Meta to lead in AI agent products that transform consumer and enterprise use cases, including agentic commerce, shaping industry economics and platform competition.

keyPoints.title: Apple's diverging user paths
keyPoints.detail: Ben Thompson explains that Apple is moving away from serving technologists and hackers toward integrated consumer products, reflecting broader trends in AI and consumer technology.

keyPoints.title: Apple and LG home partnership
keyPoints.detail: Despite Thompson's personal dissatisfaction, the partnership to expand Apple's home tech with LG aligns with the future of integrated consumer technology and is strategically sound.

keyPoints.title: Interview with Katie Harbath on tech and politics
keyPoints.detail: The conversation traces tech's early political impacts and reflects on ten years of Facebook and political backlashes, showing how business and politics have evolved intertwinedly.

keyPoints.title: The complexity of tech's political force
keyPoints.detail: Thompson and Harbath discuss the nuanced and sometimes contradictory role of technology in shaping political outcomes, acknowledging limits to tech's explanatory power.

episodes.synthesis: The episode 'It’s Not You, It’s Me' in the Stratechery series critiques the evolving relationship between Apple and its users, particularly in the context of AI and consumer technology trends. The central argument posits that Apple’s lineage as a preferred platform for both everyday consumers and technologists is fracturing due to the diverging paths of technology: one towards complete customization and the other towards full integration. Ben Thompson highlights his personal frustration with Apple’s AI stance and how Apple's venture with LG to expand its home technology offerings exemplifies a broader, successful strategic pivot—not necessarily for traditional users like himself but for the market at large. This signals a shift from what once was Apple's strength in catering to tech-savvy users toward prioritizing a different consumer ecosystem model.
episodes.whatChanged: Apple's strategic shift towards integrated home technology through partnership with LG, diverging from its traditional role as the preferred platform for technologists and hackers.
episodes.whyItMatters: This shift signals a broader market trend towards integrated consumer experiences, which may attract a larger but different user base, potentially impacting Apple's core technologist segment and altering competitive dynamics in consumer technology.

keyPoints.title: Influence of John Armitage
keyPoints.detail: Nicolai Tangen calls John Armitage one of the most important people in his life, crediting him for teaching key investing principles.

keyPoints.title: Investor Humility as a Core Value
keyPoints.detail: Discussion highlights that the best investors are humble, recognizing the limits of what they know and avoiding overconfidence.

keyPoints.title: Permanent Capital as a Trap
keyPoints.detail: John Armitage warns that permanent capital may create misaligned incentives and complacency in capital allocation, challenging the common bullish narrative.

keyPoints.title: NBIM's Concern on Declining Shareholder Rights
keyPoints.detail: NBIM views the decline in shareholder rights as a critical governance risk that threatens long-term investor value preservation.

episodes.synthesis: This episode centers on Nicolai Tangen reflecting on his former boss John Armitage's significant influence on his approach to investing and life. Armitage taught him key lessons in company analysis emphasizing investor humility and skepticism about 'permanent capital,' which Armitage considers a trap because it may distort investor incentives. The discussion also addresses a recent NBIM insight regarding the decline of shareholder rights, highlighting how this trend poses challenges for long-term institutional investors like NBIM who rely on strong governance to protect value. Beyond investing, Nicolai shares a personal perspective on gratitude, emphasizing the power of saying thank you more often and describing his morning ritual to cultivate this mindset, underscoring the episode's blend of professional wisdom and personal growth.
episodes.whatChanged: John Armitage’s perspective that permanent capital is a trap and NBIM’s warning about declining shareholder rights.
episodes.whyItMatters: These views challenge common assumptions in asset management and highlight emerging governance risks that may affect long-term investors’ ability to protect and grow capital.

keyPoints.title: AI agents to drive smartphone upgrades
keyPoints.detail: Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon predicts AI agents that use apps and personal context will trigger the next smartphone supercycle, akin to the transformative effect of early iPhone apps.

keyPoints.title: Support for 100-billion-parameter AI models on phones by 2028

keyPoints.title: Smart glasses as leading AI wearables

keyPoints.title: Qualcomm’s diverse AI device ecosystem

keyPoints.title: Interview with Katie Harbath
keyPoints.detail: Conversation with former Facebook Head of Global Elections about her book and the company's evolution in politics during the 2010s.

keyPoints.title: Facebook’s Growing Political Role in the 2010s
keyPoints.detail: Facebook shifted from a tech platform to a major political player influencing elections and political communication globally, requiring new teams and policies.

keyPoints.title: Managing Misinformation and Election Interference
keyPoints.detail: Facebook developed strategies and teams to address misinformation and election interference risks, balancing freedom of expression against political manipulation.

keyPoints.title: Changing Facebook Culture
keyPoints.detail: The company moved from optimistic connectivity to recognizing risks and regulatory pressures, developing more structured governance over political content.

episodes.synthesis: This episode features an interview with Katie Harbath, former Head of Global Elections at Facebook, discussing her new book Disrupting Politics. The central argument revolves around how Facebook's role and internal approach to politics evolved throughout the 2010s, shaping its influence and challenges in electoral processes worldwide. Harbath's insights come from her frontline experience managing political engagement on the platform as Facebook grew into a dominant force in global communications and political discourse.
episodes.whatChanged: Katie Harbath's account and book reveal how Facebook transitioned into a major political actor during the 2010s, developing new governance mechanisms to manage election interference and misinformation.
episodes.whyItMatters: This shift demonstrates the necessity for platform reform and regulation, directly impacting investments and strategies in tech companies connected to political communication and content moderation.

episodes.title: Apps, Agents, and Aggregation

keyPoints.title: Apps transitioned from standalone functions to core components of ecosystems
keyPoints.detail: Apps started as reactive tools focused on specific user tasks but evolved into essential building blocks within broader software ecosystems.

keyPoints.title: Intelligent agents enable proactive and personalized user experiences
keyPoints.detail: Agents automate decision-making and anticipate user needs, shifting software from reactive to proactive engagement, which can change user expectations and platform dynamics.

keyPoints.title: Aggregation consolidates apps and agents to drive network effects
keyPoints.detail: Platforms that successfully aggregate these elements create powerful ecosystems that capture user attention, increasing engagement and competitive moats.

keyPoints.title: Tension between platform aggregation and user desire for seamless experience
keyPoints.detail: Users prefer agent-driven, seamless interactions, but traditional aggregation treats functionalities as discrete apps, creating pressure for platforms to integrate agents more deeply.

episodes.synthesis: The central argument of the episode is that the evolution of software ecosystems hinges on the emergence of apps, intelligent agents, and aggregation models, which together redefine user interaction and platform dynamics. The episode explains how apps initially transformed user experiences by providing dedicated functions, but the rise of intelligent agents introduces a layer of proactive and personalized services that shift the role of software from reactive tools to proactive assistants. Aggregation comes into play as platforms that harness these agents and apps to consolidate user attention and engagement, creating powerful network effects and new competitive moats.
episodes.whatChanged: The key development is the recognition that integrating intelligent agents within aggregated ecosystems is the new frontier for software platform competition and user engagement.
episodes.whyItMatters: This shift means platforms must move beyond merely offering apps towards orchestrating agents that proactively serve users, creating stronger network effects and competitive moats based on personalized, anticipatory experiences.

episodes.title: Andrew Huberman - The Frontier of Neurotechnology - [Invest Like the Best, EP.494]

keyPoints.title: Neuroscience's next frontier is writing brain states
keyPoints.detail: Andrew Huberman underscores a paradigm shift from reading brain activity to precisely writing and controlling specific brain states, especially waking states critical for performance.

keyPoints.title: Waking brain states are performance bottlenecks
keyPoints.detail: Huberman explains that waking brain states dictate energy and attention, acting as bottlenecks for top performers and the key targets for neurotechnological intervention.

keyPoints.title: Leading AI companies build toward brain interfacing
keyPoints.detail: Huberman notes that companies like OpenAI and others are indirectly advancing capabilities that contribute to precise brain state modulation through integrated AI technologies.

keyPoints.title: Limitations of reading brain over writing it
keyPoints.detail: He points out that most neuroscience has been about reading brain states, limiting control; the future is precise writing to neural circuits to improve cognition and behavior.

episodes.synthesis: Andrew Huberman, a Stanford neuroscientist, argues that neuroscience is shifting from merely reading brain activity to precisely writing and controlling specific brain states. He identifies the frontier as manipulating waking brain states, which are critical for optimal performance and creativity. Huberman sees leading AI companies as unknowingly building technologies that ultimately contribute to this goal through brain-computer interaction that aims to influence brain state in nuanced ways.
episodes.whatChanged: Andrew Huberman positions the future of neuroscience as precisely writing to and controlling waking brain states, moving beyond just reading brain activity.
episodes.whyItMatters: This shift enables a new class of neurotechnologies and AI-tools that directly modulate brain energy and states, unlocking enhanced human performance and cognition, thus creating novel investable opportunities in neurotechnology and brain-AI interfaces.

episodes.title: Reflection’s founders on building a DeepSeek of the West

keyPoints.title: Beam's parameter size and training approach
keyPoints.detail: Beam is trained from scratch with 501 billion parameters, placing it among the largest open-weight models developed so far, signaling serious commitment and scale behind the project.

keyPoints.title: Beam matches top open models with higher reasoning efficiency
keyPoints.detail: Early tests put Beam alongside leading open models on coding and agent tasks, with Beam using roughly one quarter of the inference compute compared to GLM-5.3, highlighting a significant improvement in efficiency which could lower operating costs.

keyPoints.title: Apache 2.0 license enables broad developer freedom
keyPoints.detail: Beam is released under an Apache 2.0 license, allowing anyone to modify and commercially build on the model without restrictive licensing which encourages innovation and business creation around Beam.

keyPoints.title: Founders' pedigree in DeepMind projects
keyPoints.detail: CEO Misha Laskin and CTO Ioannis Antonoglou bring direct experience from Google DeepMind's Gemini, AlphaGo, and AlphaZero, lending credibility and expertise in cutting-edge AI research and reinforcement learning.

episodes.synthesis: Reflection is launching Beam, a 501 billion parameter open-weight AI model aiming to be the Western world's counterpart to China's leading open AI models. Backed by $4.6 billion in funding and valued at $25 billion, Reflection's founders have strong DeepMind pedigrees, bringing experience from leading projects Gemini, AlphaGo, and AlphaZero. Beam is notable for its efficiency, competing on coding and agent tasks while using about a quarter of the inference compute that GLM-5.3 requires, suggesting superior reasoning efficiency. Its Apache 2.0 license offers developers broad freedoms to modify and commercialize the model without restrictive licensing, marking a push toward creating an "ownership market" for AI beyond closed, rented models.

episodes.title: Noah Shinn - Building Instinct: The Personal Agent - [Invest Like the Best, EP.493]

keyPoints.title: Instinct personal assistant platform
keyPoints.detail: Instinct acts as a personal assistant with its own phone and computer, able to perform almost any online task via text, call, or email on behalf of users. Its ability to interact like a human agent is key to its rapid organic adoption.

keyPoints.title: Rapid organic growth without marketing
keyPoints.detail: Instinct is growing roughly 10% day over day without marketing spend, highlighting the strong market demand for personal agent services and effective product/market fit early in its invite-only life.

keyPoints.title: Trust-building crucial for delegation
keyPoints.detail: Noah explains how users gradually build trust to allow Instinct access to sensitive areas like credit cards and inboxes, with trust framed as fragile and critical to instilling safe delegation.

keyPoints.title: Rejection of ad revenue and alignment of incentives
keyPoints.detail: Instinct rejects ad-supported models to avoid any incentive for agents to influence users against their interests, opting instead for a take rate on $1B+ annual transactions—a business model designed to align with user benefit.

episodes.synthesis: Noah Shinn, founder of Instinct, discusses building a personal agent platform that users interact with as if texting or emailing a human assistant. Instinct has its own phone and computer capabilities and can perform virtually any online task on behalf of the user. Despite being invite-only for about a year, it is growing around 10% daily without marketing, driven by organic trust and utility. This rapid growth is supported by a trusted network allowing agents from different users to coordinate directly, enabling complex, multi-party tasks.
episodes.whatChanged: Instinct growing approximately 10% daily organically with a trusted personal assistant capable of performing nearly any online task, handling over $1 billion annually via a take rate business model.
episodes.whyItMatters: This growth demonstrates strong user demand and trust in agent-based personal assistants, signaling a disruptive shift in how consumers interact with digital services and compelling industries like travel and food delivery to adapt their customer engagement models for this new interface.

episodes.title: The Home Depot

keyPoints.title: Home Depot outperforms Apple since IPO with 25% compounding returns
keyPoints.detail: A $1,000 investment at Home Depot's 1981 IPO would be worth about $17 million today, beating Apple and making it the top S&P 500 performer over 45 years, highlighting the company's extraordinary long-term growth.

keyPoints.title: Founders fired from Handy Dan lay groundwork for Home Depot
keyPoints.detail: Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank were fired after new management took over Handy Dan, catalyzing their founding of Home Depot with the help of investor Ken Langone who backed them financially and strategically, igniting the company's creation.

keyPoints.title: Home Depot’s innovative big-box warehouse format with massive SKU count
keyPoints.detail: Home Depot pioneered large stores (around 60,000 square feet) stocking 25,000 SKUs, creating a one-stop shop experience that allowed customers to buy everything for a project in one visit with lower prices and expert service.

keyPoints.title: Equity participation creates employee motivation and wealth
keyPoints.detail: Home Depot offered stock options and discounted stock purchase programs to associates, linking their performance to company growth and creating thousands of millionaires among early employees, reinforcing culture and growth.

episodes.synthesis: Home Depot's rise from a struggling hardware store division into a $350 billion market cap retail giant is credited to a small group of founding leaders, notably Bernie Marcus, Arthur Blank, Ken Langone, and merchandising genius Pat Farrah, who combined retail savvy, financial acumen, investment banking prowess, and creative merchandising. After Bernie and Arthur were fired from their prior roles at Handy Dan, Ken Langone's investment and insider knowledge catalyzed the formation of Home Depot in 1979 with an innovative big-box warehouse concept inspired by warehouse clubs like Price Club but tailored for home improvement with massive SKU count and superb in-store expertise.
episodes.whatChanged: Ken Langone’s strategic investment in Handy Dan led to the firing of founders Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank, who then founded Home Depot with a revolutionary warehouse retail model, launching a new era in home improvement retail.
episodes.whyItMatters: This pivotal event enabled a small team with complementary skills to build a scalable and differentiated retail platform with massive SKU breadth, expert service, and employee equity, generating exceptional long-term returns and market dominance.

keyPoints.title: Disney was worth more dead than alive in 1984
keyPoints.detail: Disney Animation had stagnated and corporate raiders were targeting selling off the film library and parks, highlighting the company's troubled state.

keyPoints.title: Eisner and Wells initiated the Disney Renaissance
keyPoints.detail: Their leadership brought back the creative energy with hits like Beauty and the Beast and The Lion King, revitalizing animation and expanding the business into Broadway and home video.

keyPoints.title: CAPS technology revolutionized animation
keyPoints.detail: Computer Animation Production System (CAPS) was a pivotal innovation that enhanced animation quality and production efficiency, fueling Disney’s creative resurgence.

keyPoints.title: ESPN acquisition was a major strategic win
keyPoints.detail: Acquiring ESPN gave Disney a steady, profitable cash flow, crucial for enduring challenges and funding new initiatives.

episodes.synthesis: This episode chronicles the transformation of the Walt Disney Company from a moribund business in 1984 to the dominant media empire it became by the 21st century, led by a sequence of visionary leaders. Initially, Disney's animation studio was in decline, with corporate raiders aiming to dismantle its valuable components. The pivotal turnaround began with Michael Eisner and Frank Wells who revitalized animation through hits like Beauty and the Beast and The Lion King, while also leveraging new revenue streams such as home video, Broadway shows, and the landmark acquisition of ESPN, which became an unexpected major profit driver. However, this period was not without setbacks: Euro Disney underperformed, boardroom conflicts emerged, animation faltered significantly, and the company survived a hostile takeover attempt by Comcast. A new era commenced under Bob Iger, who restored Disney's…
episodes.whatChanged: Bob Iger’s acquisition of Pixar, Marvel, and Lucasfilm transformed Disney into a dominant 21st century media empire poised for the streaming era.
episodes.whyItMatters: These acquisitions provided Disney with critical intellectual property that secured its leadership in global media content, allowing it to effectively compete with emerging tech companies and leverage the streaming transition.
